title: Signal and Vector Again
premise: Felix Sterling has spent eleven years alone tending Earth's last seed vault and its mysterious beacon, a signal she inherited from a predecessor who vanished. When the ship Meridian returns from deep space carrying a crew aged backward into childhood, Felix discovers her beacon is the anchor dragging them home — and that it is failing. Racing to the relay at the edge of dead space, she gathers an unlikely found family among the regressed crew, learns the beacon was built by her own vanished predecessor as an inheritance meant for her, and must choose between restoring the signal that saves the children and preserving the vault's living archive. In the end Felix rewrites the beacon's code into something new: not a call back to what was lost, but a vector forward, and the family she never expected becomes the vault's true inheritance.
about_author: Ulyana Halloran is a former radio astronomer turned novelist who writes about lonely outposts and the people who refuse to abandon them. She lives above an old listening station on the northern coast, where she still keeps one antenna pointed at dead space.

chapters.title: The Caretaker's Hours
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Establishes her solitary routine in the seed vault: cataloging seeds, winding the beacon's ancient clockwork core, talking to the ghost of her predecessor, Ilsa Voss, through log entries. Emotional beat: loneliness worn smooth into ritual, and a flicker of unease when the beacon stutters for the first time in decades.

chapters.title: A Light That Answers
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. The beacon emits a return pulse no one sent. Felix traces the anomaly to coordinates in deep space and finds a ship transponder: the Meridian, lost forty years ago. Emotional beat: hope arriving like an intruder; Felix realizes someone — or something — is answering her signal.

chapters.title: Children in Vacuum Suits
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. The Meridian makes orbit, and its landing party are children wearing adult-rated suits, faces she recognizes from missing-crew archives aged backward. Their eldest, a girl named Wren, speaks with an adult's cadence. Emotional beat: wonder curdling into dread as Felix takes them in.

chapters.title: What the Vault Remembers
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The regressed crew explores the vault; Wren carries fragmented adult memories of the mission that took them to dead space. She recognizes the beacon's design. Emotional beat: grief for a self she can't reach, and the first fragile bond forming between Wren and Felix.

chapters.title: Ilsa's Last Entry
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Decoding a sealed log, Felix learns Ilsa Voss designed the beacon as a rescue anchor before vanishing toward the relay — and that the Meridian's regression was caused by time-dilation exposure near dead space. Emotional beat: betrayal and awe; Felix was chosen, not hired.

chapters.title: The Relay at the Edge
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. The beacon's failure accelerates; without repair at the relay, the Meridian's children will lose even their borrowed memories. Felix decides to make the crossing. Emotional beat: resolve hardening against fear; she packs Ilsa's notes and leaves the vault under Wren's watch.

chapters.title: Passengers
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Against orders, Wren and two of the older children stow away aboard Felix's shuttle. Discovery mid-flight forces an alliance. Emotional beat: friction becoming trust as the children prove useful, brave, and impossible to leave behind.

chapters.title: Dead Space Radio
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Crossing the boundary where signals die, the shuttle loses contact with everything behind them. Felix tells the children stories about the vault to keep panic down. Emotional beat: intimacy in isolation; the shuttle becomes a small, warm world inside the dark.

chapters.title: The Graveyard of Signals
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. They reach a debris field of ancient probes and derelict relays — every transmission humanity ever aimed at nothing, still drifting. Wren's adult memories surface violently here. Emotional beat: vertigo of inherited memory; Wren begins to understand why the ship turned back.

chapters.title: Something Is Repeating Us
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. A signal in the graveyard echoes the beacon's pulse — but older, larger, predating humanity. Something out here has been listening far longer than Ilsa knew. Emotional beat: cosmic dread tempered by Felix's stubborn caretaker instinct: you tend what you find.

chapters.title: The First Listener
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The children decode fragments suggesting the relay is not human-built but adapted from an alien structure that once broadcast a vector — a map pointing somewhere. Emotional beat: awe; the theme of inheritance expands beyond species and generations.

chapters.title: Half a Crew
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. One child, Tomas, suffers memory collapse — his regressed mind burning through its borrowed years. Felix must stabilize him using techniques from Ilsa's notes. Emotional beat: terror of failure; Felix understands she is now responsible for lives, not just seeds.

chapters.title: Arrival at the Relay
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. They dock with the relay and find it inhabited: Ilsa Voss, alive, aged forward past all recognition, sustained by the structure. Emotional beat: shock and fury; the vanished predecessor is neither savior nor villain but someone who stayed too long.

chapters.title: The Cost of Staying
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV (via recorded confession). Ilsa explains the relay's field: proximity trades your future for everyone else's past. She stayed to hold the anchor open for a ship she wasn't sure would ever come. Emotional beat: sorrowful reconciliation; sacrifice reframed as love with a terrible price.

chapters.title: Two Anchors
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Repairing the relay requires two operators — one inside the field, one outside. Ilsa is too degraded to leave; Felix realizes the role of permanent caretaker is being handed to her, exactly as Ilsa planned. Emotional beat: resistance, then the dawning choice of inheritance.

chapters.title: Wren's Vector
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren proposes the alternative: use the alien vector-map to redirect the anchor so no one must stay — but it requires broadcasting the vault's entire archive, spending Earth's stored inheritance to buy their future. Emotional beat: courage of a child thinking like the adult she lost.

chapters.title: The Vote in the Dark
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. The crew debates: preserve the archive or spend it. The children vote; Felix casts the deciding voice for spending it. Emotional beat: found family constituted by shared risk; grief and liberation entwined.

chapters.title: Broadcast
chapters.summary: Felix and Wren's alternating POV. The upload begins; the relay sings the vault's contents into the dark along the alien vector. Ilsa's anchor holds, then transforms. Tomas stabilizes as the field shifts. Emotional beat: climax — everything given away at once, and the dark giving something back.

chapters.title: An Answer Older Than Us
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. From deep beyond dead space, something answers: a coherent signal, warm and structured, acknowledging receipt. The relay's burden lifts; Ilsa can finally rest. Emotional beat: transcendence grounded in relief; they were heard.

chapters.title: Letting Go of Ilsa
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Ilsa, released from the field, ages rapidly and peacefully, entrusting the relay's codes to Felix and the children's memories to themselves. Emotional beat: mourning made gentle; inheritance accepted rather than imposed.

chapters.title: Homecoming, Rewritten
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. The shuttle returns to the vault, which is no longer a tomb but a school and a home; the Meridian's children begin growing forward again, choosing who to become. Emotional beat: belonging achieved not by returning to the old signal but by writing a new one.

chapters.title: Signal and Vector
chapters.summary: Felix's POV, years later. Felix trains Wren as the next caretaker while the vault broadcasts outward along the vector, and each season the answer from the dark comes a little closer to language. Emotional beat: quiet, earned hope — the story ends not with arrival but with a conversation just beginning.
